messages.subject_clean: AW: [unmarked] different sites within multi-season occupancy model
messages.body_plain:
Dear Rebekka,

now that’s an interesting design 😊 Seriously: you have 3 or 4 locations per stand, but you have more than just one stand, right ? Because if 3-4 sites is all you have, then I think I’d not fit these models.

When you say multi-season, do you mean the dynamic occupancy model with extinction/colonization rates ? Or do you simply want to fit separate parameters of occupancy and detection for each year ? If you have the latter, then I don’t see any problem with the change of sites in your stands, though perhaps you may still want to fit a before and after effect to accommodate any potential systematic differences between the two sets of points (especially given that there are so few of them). But if you want the former, then that one transition without any shared sites will pose a problem potentially. In the latter case, however, if you fit a model with separate extinction/colonization parameters for each annual interval, then you’re fine: you can then simply ignore the estimate from year 10 to 11, since it is probably not meaningful. However, I’d not be so comfortable to fit a model that constrains the estimates across years in some way, e.g., with a constant or with covariates across years. In that case it may be better to use a general modeling engine such as JAGS, because then you could simply treat the transitions between year 10 and 11 as separate and then model across all the remaining years ?

You can collapse your data to treat stand as a “site”. But then you lose information.

Basically, you have a multi-level design, with points nested within stand. This can be accommodated in an analysis in at least two ways. One is to focus on the point level and treat stand as a random effect. This can be done in unmarked using the TMB engine to fit such random effects. Another way would be to specify dynamics at both the stand and the point level; see this paper: Tingley, M.W., A.N. Stillman, R.L. Wilkerson, C.A. Howell, S.C. Sawyer, & R.B. Siegel. 2018. Cross-scale occupancy dynamics of a postfire specialist in response to variation across a fire regime. Journal of Animal Ecology 87:1484–1496. [link <https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1365-2656.12851>]

For this type of model you’d need JAGS or a similar generic modeling engine.

Lots of ways of looking at your design …. What’s best will also depend on your questions.

Best regards  --- Marc

I am using the colext function to run global dynamic occupancy models for several bird species. After running a mb.gof.test I see that, understandably, these models are "overdispersed". Most global models have a c-hat value ~ 2 but I have some that are ~4 and 10+.

I am trying to find a way to inflate the confidence intervals for my beta estimates, but so far have only seen c-hat incorporated into model predictions (modavgPred).

I am hoping for two things:
1. Beta estimates with c-hat inflated confidence intervals
2. Partial response values with c-hat inflated confidence intervals. I have been using predict() to get partial-response values up until this point.

As for my models with c-hat > 4, should I avoid any inference on these models altogether?

Thank you in advance to anyone who has insight,
Hannah

modavgPred( ) will produce CI's adjusted for overdispersion if you use

messages.body_plain:
Since my last post I've gone back to the example script I started with (found here: https://rdrr.io/cran/unmarked/man/gmultmix.html) and experimented with running gmultmix() models using simulated datasets. Basically, the model throws this error:

Error in optim(starts, nll, method = method, hessian = se, ...) :
  initial value in 'vmmin' is not finite

anytime the true abundance (in the data simulation code) is set to >50. This can be resolved by increasing K until I set abundance > 196, at which point increasing K to even absurdly large values (100k, 1 million, 5 million, 50 million, 100 million) doesn't seem to have any impact.
Incidentally, when I tried K values of 100 million, I got this error, so I didn't try anything larger:
Error: cannot allocate vector of size 14.9 Gb
I'm using a machine with 64 Gb of RAM, so I'm not sure where the size limit is coming from.

So. Given these patterns, I'm hoping someone out there who better understands the inner workings of unmarked can help me figure out whether there is something that can be done to resolve the problem.

Below is the code for simulating data and running a simple null model that I found at the link above:

library(unmarked)
# Simulate data using the multinomial-Poisson model with a repeated constant-interval removal design.
n <- 100  # number of sites
T <- 4    # number of primary periods
J <- 3    # number of secondary periods
lam <- 100 #### this is what i've been changing the true abundance for the simulated population
phi <- 0.5
p <- 0.3
y <- array(NA, c(n, T, J))
M <- rpois(n, lam)          # Local population size
N <- matrix(NA, n, T)       # Individuals available for detection
for(i in 1:n) {
  N[i,] <- rbinom(T, M[i], phi)
  y[i,,1] <- rbinom(T, N[i,], p)    # Observe some
  Nleft1 <- N[i,] - y[i,,1]         # Remove them
  y[i,,2] <- rbinom(T, Nleft1, p)
  Nleft2 <- Nleft1 - y[i,,2]
  y[i,,3] <- rbinom(T, Nleft2, p)
}
y.ijt <- cbind(y[,1,], y[,2,], y[,3,], y[,4,])
umf1 <- unmarkedFrameGMM(y=y.ijt, numPrimary=T, type="removal")
(m1 <- gmultmix(~1, ~1, ~1, data=umf1, K=1000))   #### this is where I've been changing K

Hi Jillian,

Your example code runs fine for me (I tried a few different simulation runs). I'm not sure if you meant that example  to work or not work?

K needs to be at least equal to the "known" minimum population size, which in a removal dataset would be the sum of all the removal counts at a site (i.e., you know at least that many animals must have existed). At the moment however the default is to use the max of any single count + 100. If your removal counts are relatively small, this shouldn't be a problem, but if they are occasionally very large, the auto-generated K might not be big enough and lead to optimization issues like you saw. The solution is to manually set K to at least be as big as the max total number you removed from a site plus a big buffer, which it sounds like is what you figured out. The way K is generated by default should be fixed for gmultmix I think.

You don't need to keep making K bigger and bigger, as long as it is "big enough" you should get the same results as you noticed. So just find a value that works and try a few larger values until you are sure the estimates have stabilized. For lam = 100 for example, K=1000 should be plenty high.

As far as your memory issue goes I'm not surprised. If you make K = 100 million, unmarked is generating some really large vectors and matrices to feed into the optimization which take up tons of memory. Also, while I don't know the reasons exactly, it is pretty typical in my experience to get R crashes when you have used much less than your theoretical maximum RAM. But you shouldn't ever have to set K that high (I guess unless you were working with bacteria or something, and if so unmarked is probably not the right tool).

Ken

In the function that's used to calculate the log-likelihood, there is one particular calculation that when counts and K are large, the intermediate result can be so large (basically exp(some large number)) that it is simply considered infinite instead. I *think* if the algorithm used here was structured differently, this might be avoided. I will look into that, but it might take a while.

If Richard sees this maybe he has more comments on using relatively large counts with this function - I think it has mainly been used with e.g. bird point counts where the numbers involved typically stay smaller.

Ken

I have maybe a minority viewpoint on including (I suppose you mean "highly" rather than "perfectly") collinear covariates in models (whether they be in the occupancy or detection part or both):

1. If you're only interested in prediction and the software doesn't run into numerical convergence issues, use all the variables you have available or are cheap to measure or you simply have access to (but with a rational model building process - i.e., starting with simpler or theoretically reasonable models).

2.  Throwing out highly collinear covariates doesn't fix a collinear problem:  doing so just ignores the problem.  Interpretation of the coefficients of those variables included in the model would still be suspect if the excluded covariates aren't explained away with explicit justification.  (Throwing out a more expensive covariate that is replaced by a relatively cheaper-to-measure or more-readily-available covariate where both covariates are highly correlated would be one kind of justification.)

Jim

messages.subject: A comment on model complexity in occupancy and similar models
messages.subject_clean: A comment on model complexity in occupancy and similar models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

this is a comment motivated by a recent post on this list where a model with 10 or so covariates was fit to occupancy data from 20 sites. This is asking FAR too much from the data !

We should never forget that a static occupancy or Nmix model can be viewed as the combination of two regression models: one for occupancy/abundance and the other for detection. So, we can only estimate so many parameters from so much data. In the general regression literature one can find rules of thumb that for every parameter in a regression model, one needs, say, 5-10 data points. So this would then suggest that with 20 sites, one should estimate at most 4 parameters in the state model. This could be one intercept plus 3 slopes for instance.

But the situation is even worse: while in a simple regression, these data points are observed, in a regression for occupancy probability, the implied data points are the latent presence/absence states of each site. These are not even observed, or only partially so (in the no-false-positive models we assume that the 1's are observed); rather, we must estimate the data points in the model. So we have even less information. This might then suggest that in a model fit to 20 sites we should perhaps not estimate more than 2 or 3 parameters in the state model at most.

We are in a slightly better situation for the observation model. Due to the repeated-measures nature of the data, there is more information on the detection part of the model; plus, the data are actually observed rather than partially latent. Hence, with 20 sites and, say, 3 visits at each, our sample size relevant for estimation of detection is 60, and then we may try to fit perhaps up to 5-10 parameters in the observation model.

I admit that I have disregarded these recommendations myself from time to time. But I think they are important as a benchmark when working with these models.

Best regards  -- Marc

Dear all,

I am intending to use unmarked for running single-season occupancy models on detection/nondetection data on striped hyenas collected in a human dominated landscape in western India. Having gone through Fiske & Chandler 2011 and the vignettes, I have two questions which are rather basic, so I apologize if these have already been covered by the above material:

i) How do I generate heat maps of occupancy probabilities given a map of the study area? Of course, I could obtain the corresponding probabilities based on the best fitting model/model averaged values and the covariate values at each site and then map the data on R or a GIS platform, but I wanted to know if there is any functionality in unmarked that would make the process simpler.

ii) Does unmarked accommodate the Hines et al. 2010 model, which deals with spatially autocorrelated detections across replicates? In my study, the replicates were contiguous segments of transects 200-300m long, and I anticipate that hyenas may have moved across contiguous segments, and thus I would like to use this model.

I would be highly grateful if these queries could be addressed at the earliest.

Best Regards,

Soumya Banerjee,
Junior Research Fellow,
Wildlife Institute of India,
Dehradun, Uttarakhand, India

messages.subject_clean: N-mixture Community Models without lambda covariates and with probable site heterogeneity in abundance
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone

I have data

collected under a removal sampling protocol for several tropical bat species along an elevation gradient in Brazil and would like to run Community N-Mixture multinomial models (as in Chandler et al. 2013, Conservation Biology) for the sole purpose of: obtaining estimates of the abundance of each species corrected for variations in detectability. From this estimates, we will calculate metrics like species richness, community size, sites (dis)similarity, etc.
The knowledge that my colleagues and I have about the system and study group allows us to state that: (i) the abundance of all species is affected by the gradient, and it is likely that no species inhabits the areas of higher elevation; (ii) on nights below 10º C the activity of bats strongly decreases due to mechanisms such as torpor, and about 20% of our samplings were under these conditions.

Under these assumptions, the most obvious initial step would be to model these data using elevation and temperature as covariates of lambda and p, respectively. However, there is a problem: Including elevation as a covariate would lead to circularity in some analyzes that we will do later (variance partitioning, regression on distance matrices, among others), where elevation will be used as a predictor along with spatial, connectivity, among others variables. On the other hand, ignoring the effect of elevation seems to me to be the case of the unmodeled site heterogeneity in abundance discussed in chap. 6.7 of the AHM book, and which would therefore bias the estimates (table 6.2 of the book).

So my question is: Is there any way to get unbiased abundance estimates in this case, without including elevation as a covariate of lambda? Would including "site" as a categorical covariate for lambda be an option?

Carlos

messages.body_plain:
Dear Carlos,

I find this an excellent question; I have often wondered about this. My feeling is exactly the same as yours: if you use the same covariate, such as elevation in your case, both in the Nmix model and then again in a 2nd step analysis that uses as input an estimate from the Nmix, then that smells like double use of the same data, circularity etc. But if you don't use the covariate in the first step, then bad things may happen.

I don't see any immediate solution to this conundrum. Perhaps you can run some simulations to study this situation and get a feel for what is better: ignoring an important covariate in the first step of the analysis or do some double-dipping ? You could simulate a simple community data set with effects of one covariate, fit an Nmix with and without use of elevation as a covariate and compare the inferences from some 2nd stage analyses. Part of me thinks that using the same covariate twice may only lead to SEs that will be too small. Perhaps that is not as bad as getting substantial bias ?

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
I agree with you, Jim. An N-mix model containing variables representing niche selection, drift and dispersal limitation would be the most suitable.
Niche selection (at least environmental filtering) can be addressed by including environmental covariates for lambda, of course. Dispersal limitation could perhaps be included in the model through variables representing spatial autocorrelation in abundances, and I believe this has already been done (I remember reading it somewhere). I just have no idea how to add ecological drift hypothesis to the model. Many drift predictions are based on community size (sum of the abundance of all species; see Vellend, 2016). For example: greater variation (i.e. beta diversity) in smaller communities; weaker species-environment relationships in smaller communities, among other things. This is complex because community size would also be a product of the Community N-mix, so it is difficult for me to think of ways to test such predictions in an analysis that is not post-fitting the model.

Dear Carlos,

ideally, such a simulation would allow one to specify a covariate with some effect A on the abundance of a single species and then to have another effect B on some feature of community composition. Then, you could switch on and off A or B in the data generation, and add in the analysis the covariate in the first or the second steps, and see which approach does best. But this would be a major paper project.

It might also be possible to develop a big model that does abundance estimation and community analysis all in one step. But that sounds like an even bigger project.

As to your questions: it may be that adopting a NegBin abundance mixture, without covariates, might improve the estimates, but I am not sure. At any rate, in an Nmix model, both the NegBin and the Poisson-lognormal (PLN) distributions are a way to allow site abundance to be more variable than what a Poisson allows. They are not the same models, but will typically yield similar inferences. When specifying models in the BUGS language I usually prefer the PLN because I perceive it as being conceptually simpler.

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
In all cases the estimated occupancy intercept is very large, which means the model is estimating occupancy probability to be 1 (plogis(some large number) = 1). Given the information about your dataset that I have, I am not surprised. You have a very small number of detections relative to the number of observations (~5%) which means detection probability will likely be very small (which the model results do show) and thus occupancy will be very high. This is especially true because you detected the species at least once at most of the sites (~60%).

My conclusion is that you are unlikely to get useful occupancy results from this dataset, at least using unmarked. The data are unfortunately just too sparse. It is not a good idea to use parameter estimates from unmarked when occupancy is estimated at 1 and/or there are issues getting the standard errors. I am guessing the occupancy intercepts are very large even for the other models where the SEs are not NaN.

I'm not sure what your observations represent (individual days?), but you could try collapsing your y matrix into a smaller number of longer observation periods e.g. weeks instead of days taking care that you still meet the assumptions of occupancy modeling in your study system such as population closure.

You may have more success fitting the model in a Bayesian framework, although I would expect the results in this case to be strongly influenced by the prior distributions for better or worse.

Ken

Dear Ken, Thank you very much for your insights, That makes perfect sense.

Let me give you a better overview. I have run the test with the same camera deployed for wolf, and the numbers were very nice and compliant with my hypothesis and model assumptions.

It looked like a paradox that yaks, which could be recorded all the time in the camera, have worse predictive quality.

I wanted to support the fact that wolves' occupancy showed a positive response to altitude. I tried to find a reason for this result in a higher presence of yaks and shepherds at lower locations.
The observation events are based on daily records, yes. I will try to probe as you mentioned smaller but longer observations.

In case it does not work, would you recommend me a test to check on altitude influence in this type of data?

Again, you saved my life with this reply. Thank you very very much for your time and your kindness.

Given the information about your dataset that I have, I am not surprised. You have a very small number of detections relative to the number of observations (~5%) which means detection probability will likely be very small (which the model results do show) and thus occupancy will be very high. This is especially true because you detected the species at least once at most of the sites (~60%).

It is not a good idea to use parameter estimates from unmarked when occupancy is estimated at 1 and/or there are issues getting the standard errors. I am guessing the occupancy intercepts are very large even for the other models where the SEs are not NaN.

>
